title: Decision Trees
oneLiner: A flowchart of yes/no questions, chosen so each question removes as much uncertainty as possible.

what.html:
A decision tree is a flowchart of questions. Each internal node asks about one attribute ("Is the outlook sunny?"), each branch is an answer, and each leaf gives a decision ("Play tennis: yes").

Everyday versionThe game "20 questions". A good player asks the question that splits the possibilities most evenly first ("Is it alive?"), not a narrow one ("Is it a giraffe?"). A decision tree learner does exactly this with data.

Reading a path from root to leaf gives a rule: IF Outlook = Sunny AND Humidity = Normal THEN Yes. The whole tree is an OR of such rules.

why.html:
• They explain themselves. You can show the tree to a manager or a doctor.
  • They are cheap and fast to build and to use, and handle mixed data (categories and numbers).
  • They ignore irrelevant attributes automatically: a useless column simply never gets chosen.
  • They are the building block of random forests and boosting (Module 9), among the strongest methods for tabular data.

how.title: Measure surprise: information
how.html: Rare news carries more information than expected news. "It snowed in Chennai" tells you more than "it was hot in Chennai". Mathematically, the information in an event with probability p is log₂(1/p) bits.

how.title: Measure mess: entropy
how.html: Entropy is the average surprise of a group. A basket with only apples has entropy 0 (no uncertainty). A 50/50 mix of apples and oranges has entropy 1 bit (maximum uncertainty for two classes). A 9-to-5 mix is in between: 0.94.

how.title: Pick the question that tidies up most
how.html:
Information gain = mess before the question − average mess after it (weighted by group size). Try each attribute; the one with the largest gain becomes the question at this node.

On the slides' tennis data, Outlook wins at the root (gain 0.246), because the Overcast branch is already perfectly "Yes".

how.title: Repeat on each branch: ID3
how.html: Split the data by the chosen question, then repeat on each branch with the remaining attributes. Stop when a branch is pure, when attributes run out (take a majority vote), or when no examples are left.

how.title: Use the tree
how.html: To classify a new day, start at the root and follow the answers: Sunny → Humidity High → No. Judge the tree on data it hasn't seen, using the confusion matrix from Module 4.

how.title: Numbers: choose a threshold
how.html: For a number like income, turn it into a yes/no question "income ≤ c?". Sort the values, try thresholds halfway between neighbours, and keep the one whose split is purest. For the slides' borrowers, "income ≤ 97.5K" is best.

how.title: Trees love to memorise
how.html: Keep splitting and a tree can carve a tiny box around every training point, including noise. Training error drops to 0 while test error rises. That's overfitting.

how.title: Prune before or after
how.html:
• Pre-pruning: stop early, e.g. don't split if the gain is below a threshold, if the tree is too deep, or if a node has too few examples.
  • Post-pruning: grow the full tree, then walk back up and remove any branch whose removal doesn't hurt accuracy on a separate "prune set".

how.title: Another mess-meter: Gini
how.html: The Gini index is the chance that two random picks from a group disagree on the class. Like entropy it is 0 for a pure group; it is cheaper to compute and is the default in scikit-learn (CART).

how.title: Don't be fooled by ID-like columns
how.html: A "customer ID" column splits every row into its own pure group, so its information gain is maximal, yet it's useless for prediction. Gain ratio divides the gain by how many ways the attribute splits the data, penalising such attributes.

how.title: Prefer the simplest explanation
how.html: The Minimum Description Length principle picks the tree that gives the shortest total message: describe the tree, plus describe its mistakes. A small tree with a few errors can beat a big tree with none. It's Occam's razor made measurable.

demo.html: Build the tennis tree yourself. At each highlighted node the panel lists the information gain of every remaining attribute. Pick one (the best is marked) and the node splits. Keep going until every leaf is pure. Then try picking a poor attribute first and compare the size of the tree you end up with.

example.html:
Loan defaults. The slides' borrower table (home owner, marital status, annual income → defaulted?) is a classic credit-risk tree: home owners never defaulted, and among non-owners, marital status and income separate the rest.

Listed applications: biomedical, manufacturing, banking, make-or-buy decisions.

Supplementary In network operations, a tree over alarm attributes (vendor, alarm type, time since last change, KPI drop) gives engineers readable rules for which alarms need a site visit.

misunderstandings: The deepest tree is the most accurate.
It fits noise; test error rises after a point.
Highest information gain is always the best attribute.
Not for ID-like attributes with many values; use gain ratio.
Trees find the best possible tree.
They grow greedily, one split at a time; the globally best tree is usually not found.
Splits compare values to thresholds, so scaling doesn't matter.
takeaways: A tree is a set of if-then rules: OR of AND conditions.
Entropy measures impurity; information gain = entropy before − weighted entropy after.
ID3 greedily picks the highest-gain attribute and recurses until leaves are pure.
Numeric attributes get a threshold; Gini is an alternative impurity; gain ratio handles many-valued attributes.
Trees overfit easily: pre-prune, post-prune with a validation set, or apply MDL.
thirty: A decision tree is a flowchart of questions learned from data. At each node, it chooses the attribute that most reduces impurity, measured by entropy (information gain) or the Gini index, then repeats on each branch until the leaves are pure. Numbers are split at the best threshold, and gain ratio stops ID-like attributes from winning unfairly. Because trees can memorise noise, we limit or prune them using a validation set or the minimum description length principle.

check.q: Entropy of a group with 7 positives and 7 negatives is…
check.why: A 50/50 split of two classes has maximum entropy, 1 bit.

check.q: Which attribute does ID3 choose at a node?
opts: The one with the most values
The one with highest information gain

check.q: A tree with zero training error and high test error is…
Why can 'Customer ID' get the highest information gain?
opts: Each ID forms a pure group of one
Removing it doesn't increase error on a prune set
